item.title: DPIN: Deep Page-Level Interest Network for Ad Allocation at Meituan via Reinforcement Learning (SIGIR 2022)
item.description:
Meituan deployed DPIN (Deep Page-level Interest Network) for ad allocation using reinforcement learning, effectively modeling page-level user preference to maximize overall revenue. The paper was accepted as a short paper at SIGIR 2022.

Previous works only modeled user's historical point-level positive feedback (clicks), neglecting the page-level information. DPIN addresses this by incorporating multiple types of feedback at the page level — considering the entire page of items (both ads and organic content) rather than individual items in isolation.

The core module is a multi-channel interaction module that captures user preferences for item arrangements under different receptive fields. This models how users scan and interact with pages of content, not just individual items. Four different types of page-level feedback are used as input.

The system allocates limited ad slots to maximize overall revenue in mixed lists of ads and organic items. This is fundamentally different from pointwise CTR prediction — the value of showing an ad depends on what else is on the page, the user's browsing pattern, and the position of the ad.

The deployment on Meituan's food delivery platform demonstrates that page-level modeling delivers improvements over pointwise approaches. The reinforcement learning framework allows the system to learn optimal ad allocation policies that balance short-term revenue with long-term user satisfaction.

For practitioners, DPIN highlights the importance of page-level context in ad allocation. Modeling the entire page — not just individual ad impressions — can capture important signals about user behavior and optimize for page-level objectives like total revenue or user experience.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.00377

item.title: Delayed Feedback in CTR Prediction: 55% RPM Gain via Neural Network Loss Functions (RecSys 2019)
item.description:
Researchers from Twitter published a study on addressing delayed feedback for continuous training with neural networks in CTR prediction, achieving 3% relative RCE improvement offline and 55% RPM gain against naive log loss online. The paper was accepted at RecSys 2019.

In display advertising, positive labels (conversions) are only observed after a possibly long and random delay. A naive approach treating missing labels as negative tends to underestimate CTR, resulting in inferior user experience and lost revenue. This is a fundamental challenge for continuous training where fresh data lacks complete labels.

The paper compares both shallow and deep model architectures and benchmarks 5 different loss functions, with 3 of them applied to this problem for the first time. Training data scale was 668 million in-house data points for offline experiments.

The 55% RPM gain against naive log loss is dramatic. RPM (Revenue Per Thousand Requests) improvement means the platform generates significantly more revenue from the same traffic. This demonstrates that how you handle delayed feedback has a massive impact on business outcomes.

The paper also discusses the engineering cost associated with implementing each loss function in a production environment — an important practical consideration that is often overlooked in research papers. Some loss functions may be theoretically superior but too complex or expensive to implement in production.

For practitioners, this work highlights that the delayed feedback problem is one of the most impactful issues in ad tech ML. The choice of loss function for handling delayed conversions can make or break a CTR model's performance. The 55% RPM improvement from using the right loss function versus naive log loss is one of the largest improvements reported in the ad tech literature.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.06558

item.title: GR4AD: Generative Recommendation at Scale in Kuaishou Advertising
item.description:
Generative recommendation has moved from research curiosity to production system. Kuaishou's GR4AD (Generative Recommendation for Advertising) is one of the first large-scale deployments of autoregressive generative models in an ad platform, and the engineering choices are instructive for anyone considering this direction.

The core challenge is that generative recommendation requires tokenizing items into semantic IDs, running an autoregressive decoder, and serving results under real-time latency constraints — none of which traditional DLRM pipelines were designed for. GR4AD addresses this with several co-designed components.

Unified Advertisement Semantic IDs (UA-SID) tokenize ads by capturing business-relevant attributes — category, brand, price tier, engagement signals — into discrete codes. This replaces the standard embedding table lookup with a structured tokenization that the autoregressive model can condition on. The key design choice is making the semantic IDs encode commercial information, not just content similarity, so the generation process is inherently value-aware.

LazyAR relaxes layer-wise autoregressive dependencies for short, multi-candidate generation. In standard autoregressive decoding, each token depends on all previous tokens — expensive when generating multiple candidates. LazyAR decouples this for the candidate generation stage, reducing inference cost while preserving ranking quality. This is critical because ad retrieval needs to generate hundreds of candidates per request within single-digit millisecond budgets.

On the training side, the team introduced two techniques. Value-Aware Supervised Learning (VSL) incorporates ad value signals directly into the supervised training objective, so the model learns to generate high-value candidates rather than just high-relevance ones. Ranking-Guided Softmax Preference Optimization (RSPO) is a list-wise RL algorithm that optimizes for ranking-aware rewards — essentially training the generative model to produce candidate lists that, when ranked downstream, maximize system-level metrics.

For serving, dynamic beam serving adapts beam width across generation levels and current online load. During peak traffic, the system narrows the beam to meet latency SLOs; during off-peak, it expands to improve recall. This compute-adaptive approach is a practical necessity for any generative model serving at scale.

Results: Online A/B tests showed up to 4.2% ad revenue improvement over the existing DLRM-based system. The gains came from both model scaling (larger architectures) and inference-time scaling (wider beams when compute permits). The system is fully deployed serving over 400 million users.

Practical implications: This paper demonstrates that generative recommendation can beat well-tuned DLRM pipelines at scale, but only with significant co-design across tokenization, architecture, training, and serving. The LazyAR and dynamic beam components are particularly relevant — naive autoregressive decoding would never meet ad serving latency requirements. Teams exploring generative retrieval for ads should study the serving architecture as closely as the model itself.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.22732

item.title: DSTN: Deep Spatio-Temporal Neural Networks for CTR Prediction at Shenma Search (KDD 2019)
item.description:
Shenma Search (China's second largest search engine) deployed DSTN (Deep Spatio-Temporal Neural Networks) for CTR prediction. The best-performing variant was deployed in production, with A/B testing confirming that online CTR was significantly improved compared to the previous serving model. The paper was accepted at KDD 2019.

Traditional CTR prediction treats each ad independently, ignoring its relationship to other ads that may impact the CTR. DSTN incorporates two types of auxiliary information:

  • Spatial Domain: Considers contextual ads shown above the target ad on the same page. This captures the intuition that ads shown together may influence each other — a user might click an ad because it was the best option among the displayed ads.
  • Temporal Domain: Considers historically clicked ads (reflecting user preferences) and historically unclicked ads (indicating what a user dislikes). Both positive and negative signals contribute to understanding user intent.

The model learns interactions between each type of auxiliary data and the target ad, can emphasize more important hidden information, and performs fusion of heterogeneous data in a unified framework.

Experiments on one public dataset and two industrial datasets showed DSTN outperforms several state-of-the-art methods for CTR prediction. The deployment at Shenma Search validates that spatio-temporal modeling delivers real improvements in production search advertising.

For practitioners, DSTN demonstrates that the context in which an ad appears — both spatially (what other ads are shown) and temporally (what the user has interacted with before) — contains important signal for CTR prediction. Most CTR models focus on the target ad and user features, but DSTN shows that auxiliary ad context can significantly improve predictions.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.03776

item.title: TFNet: Multi-Semantic Feature Interaction for CTR Prediction at Tencent MyApp (SIGIR 2020)
item.description:
Tencent deployed TFNet (Tensor-based Feature interaction Network) for CTR prediction in MyApp, the largest Chinese app recommender system. Online A/B tests achieved large improvement of revenue and click rate. The paper was accepted at SIGIR 2020.

TFNet introduces an operating tensor to elaborate feature interactions via multi-slice matrices in multiple semantic spaces. The key insight is that prior methods generally use the vector-product of each pair of features, ignoring the different semantic spaces in which features operate.

By modeling feature interactions across multiple semantic spaces simultaneously, TFNet captures richer patterns than single-space approaches. The tensor-based interaction mechanism allows the model to learn that the same pair of features may interact differently depending on the semantic context.

Offline experiments on the Criteo and Avazu datasets showed TFNet outperforms competitive methods including Logistic Regression, Factorization Machines, Wide&Deep, Neural Factorization Machines, and DeepFM. The deployment in Tencent MyApp — serving hundreds of millions of users — validates that these improvements translate to real business impact.

For practitioners, TFNet demonstrates that feature interaction modeling can be improved by considering multiple semantic spaces. Most CTR models use a single interaction mechanism (inner product, element-wise product, or cross network), but TFNet shows that different interaction types capture different patterns and combining them improves overall performance.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.15939

item.title: MVKE: Mixture of Virtual-Kernel Experts for Multi-Objective User Profile Modeling at Tencent (KDD 2022)
item.description:
Tencent deployed MVKE (Mixture of Virtual-Kernel Experts) for multi-objective user profile modeling in their advertising system. The system brought about an obvious lift to actual advertising revenue. The paper was accepted at SIGKDD 2022.

MVKE addresses the limitation of traditional Two-Tower models, which use multiple independent models to predict user actions on different tags. Single-action models cannot learn complementarily and support effective training on data-sparse actions. The lack of information fusion between towers causes insufficient learning of user preferences across various tag topics.

The core concept is Virtual-Kernel Experts — each focuses on modeling one particular facet of the user's preferences, learning coordinately. A gate-based structure builds an information fusion bridge between the two towers, addressing the traditional limitation of no cross-tower information sharing.

The multi-task design learns user preferences across multiple actions (click, conversion) and multiple tag topics jointly, rather than using independent single-action models. This enables knowledge sharing across tasks — a user who clicks on sports content may also be more likely to convert on sports-related ads.

The gate structure maintains high efficiency while improving capability, which is critical for production ad systems where serving latency is a hard constraint.

For practitioners, MVKE demonstrates that the Two-Tower architecture can be enhanced with cross-tower information sharing without sacrificing serving efficiency. The virtual-kernel expert approach is a practical way to model multi-faceted user preferences in a multi-task learning framework.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.07356

item.title: FAT: Field-Aware Transformer with First Scaling Law for CTR Prediction: +2.33% CTR, +0.66% RPM
item.description:
Researchers published FAT (Field-Aware Transformer), which presents the first formal scaling law for CTR models, grounded in Rademacher complexity. Online deployment showed +2.33% CTR and +0.66% RPM improvements. Offline benchmarks showed up to +0.51% AUC over state-of-the-art.

FAT identifies a structural misalignment between standard Transformers and CTR data. Transformers assume sequential compositionality, while CTR data demand combinatorial reasoning over high-cardinality semantic fields. Unstructured attention distributes capacity broadly, amplifying noise under sparse conditions.

The architecture embeds field-based interaction priors directly into the attention mechanism using two core components: decomposed content alignment and cross-field modulation. Model complexity scales with the number of fields F, rather than total vocabulary size n >> F, yielding tighter generalization bounds.

The theoretical contribution is significant: the paper demonstrates that AUC follows a power-law scaling pattern as model width increases. This is the first formal scaling law for CTR models, analogous to the scaling laws discovered for language models. The finding suggests that there is a principled way to predict how model improvements will translate to accuracy gains.

The core thesis is that effective scaling in recommendation arises not from size, but from structured expressivity — emphasizing architectural coherence with data semantics over raw model size. This challenges the trend toward simply making CTR models larger.

For practitioners, FAT provides two key insights: (1) field-aware attention is superior to standard attention for CTR data, and (2) there exists a predictable scaling law that can guide model development decisions. The 2.33% CTR and 0.66% RPM improvements demonstrate that these theoretical insights translate to real business impact.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.12081

item.title: GPSD: Scaling Transformers for Discriminative Recommendation via Generative Pretraining (KDD 2025)
item.description:
Researchers published GPSD (Generative Pretraining for Scalable Discriminative Recommendation), a framework that uses generative model parameters to initialize discriminative CTR/CVR models. The approach enables consistent performance gains as models scale from 13K to 0.3B dense parameters, closely adhering to power laws. The paper was accepted at KDD 2025.

The core problem is that discriminative recommendation tasks suffer from significant overfitting due to data sparsity. Larger discriminative models paradoxically underperform smaller ones because overfitting worsens with size. Generative training, however, shows no evident signs of overfitting.

GPSD addresses this by using parameters from a pretrained generative model to initialize a discriminative model, then applying a sparse parameter freezing strategy. This substantially narrows the generalization gap in model training, resulting in better test performance.

The approach leverages the scalability of Transformers, delivering consistent performance gains as models are scaled up. Online A/B tests showed remarkable improvements, validating that these techniques work in production.

The broader implication is unifying the architectures of recommendation models and language models, enabling transfer of LLM techniques to recommendation systems. This represents a convergence of the two fields that could accelerate progress in ad tech.

For practitioners, GPSD demonstrates that generative pretraining — the same technique that enabled the LLM revolution — can improve CTR/CVR prediction models. The key insight is that generative training learns robust representations that generalize better than discriminative training alone, especially when data is sparse.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.03699

item.title: Uni-CTR: Unified Multi-Domain CTR Prediction via LLMs with Zero-Shot Capability (ACM TOIS)
item.description:
Researchers published Uni-CTR, a unified framework for multi-domain CTR prediction using large language models. The framework outperforms state-of-the-art multi-domain CTR models significantly on three public datasets and demonstrates remarkable effectiveness in zero-shot prediction. The paper was accepted at ACM Transactions on Information Systems (TOIS).

Multi-domain CTR prediction suffers from the "seesaw phenomenon" where models get dominated by some specific domains, causing performance drops in others. Traditional approaches encode domains as discrete identifiers, ignoring rich semantic information about what makes each domain unique.

Uni-CTR uses a backbone LLM that learns layer-wise semantic representations capturing commonalities between domains, combined with domain-specific networks that capture the characteristics of each domain. A critical design choice is the masked loss strategy, which decouples domain-specific networks from the backbone LLM.

This decoupling means domain-specific networks remain unchanged when incorporating new or removing domains, enhancing flexibility and scalability. This is valuable for advertising platforms that frequently add new ad products or surfaces.

The zero-shot capability is particularly important — Uni-CTR can make reasonable predictions for domains with limited or no training data by leveraging the LLM's semantic understanding of domain characteristics. This addresses the cold-start problem that plagues multi-domain systems.

For practitioners, Uni-CTR demonstrates that LLMs can serve as a backbone for multi-domain CTR prediction, providing semantic understanding that enables better domain generalization and zero-shot transfer. The masked loss strategy for decoupling domain-specific components is a practical technique for building scalable multi-domain systems.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.10743

item.title: IDProxy: Cold-Start CTR Prediction via Multimodal LLM Proxy Embeddings at Xiaohongshu
item.description:
Cold-start remains one of the most persistent problems in ad ranking. When a new item enters the system, it has no interaction history, making its ID embedding essentially random. Xiaohongshu's IDProxy tackles this by using multimodal large language models to generate proxy embeddings that substitute for missing ID embeddings during the cold-start phase.

The core idea is straightforward: if you can't learn an item's embedding from user interactions, generate one from its content — images, title text, category metadata. What makes IDProxy technically interesting is how it bridges the gap between the MLLM's representation space and the ranking model's ID embedding space.

The system extracts multimodal features from item content using a pretrained MLLM, then projects them through a learned alignment layer to produce proxy embeddings. These proxies are explicitly aligned with the existing ID embedding space — not just in terms of dimensionality, but in terms of the geometric structure that the ranking model expects. The alignment is trained end-to-end under CTR objectives together with the ranking model, so the proxy embeddings are optimized for the downstream prediction task rather than generic content similarity.

This end-to-end optimization is the key architectural decision. Earlier cold-start approaches would pre-compute content embeddings independently and then either concatenate them with ID embeddings or use them as initialization. IDProxy instead treats the MLLM as a feature extractor within the ranking pipeline, allowing gradients from the CTR loss to flow back through the alignment layer and shape the proxy embeddings to be maximally useful for ranking.

A practical subtlety: the system needs to handle the transition from cold-start to warm state. As an item accumulates interactions, its learned ID embedding becomes more informative than the proxy. IDProxy manages this gracefully — the proxy serves as a warm initialization that gets refined by actual user signals, rather than a hard cutoff between proxy and learned embeddings.

Deployment: IDProxy is live in both Xiaohongshu's Content Feed and Display Ads features, serving hundreds of millions of users daily. The paper reports effectiveness in both offline experiments and online A/B tests, though specific lift numbers are not disclosed in the abstract.

Why this matters: For ad platforms with large catalogs of new or long-tail items (e-commerce, classified ads, creator marketplaces), cold-start CTR prediction directly impacts revenue. IDProxy's approach of aligning MLLM representations with the ranking model's embedding space — rather than treating them as separate systems — is a pattern likely to become standard. The technical challenge is keeping the alignment layer stable as the ranking model evolves; any retraining of the base ranking model can shift the target embedding space and require re-alignment.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.01590

item.title: AdNanny: A Unified Reasoning LLM for Offline Advertising Tasks at Bing Ads
item.description:
Large language models are powerful but expensive to deploy in latency-constrained ad serving. Microsoft's AdNanny takes a different approach: instead of trying to use LLMs in the real-time ranking path, it uses a single fine-tuned LLM as a unified backbone for offline advertising tasks — labeling, scoring, content moderation, and other batch processes where latency is measured in seconds, not milliseconds.

The base model is a 671B-parameter DeepSeek-R1 checkpoint, fine-tuned with hybrid dense-MoE parallelism. The training recipe has two stages. First, multi-task supervised fine-tuning with adaptive reweighting — the system balances training signal across different offline tasks, preventing high-volume tasks from drowning out lower-volume but equally important ones. Second, reinforcement learning using downstream advertising metrics — the model is further optimized against actual business metrics (not just cross-entropy) so its outputs are calibrated for ad system needs.

The reasoning-augmented training data is a notable design choice. Rather than just input-output pairs, the training corpora pair structured supervision with step-by-step natural language explanations. This chain-of-thought format improves the model's ability to handle edge cases and ambiguous inputs — critical for tasks like ad content moderation where the rules are nuanced and context-dependent.

The practical impact is consolidating many task-specific models into a single backbone. Before AdNanny, Bing Ads maintained separate models for different offline tasks, each with its own training pipeline, data requirements, and serving infrastructure. AdNanny replaces these with one model that handles multiple tasks, significantly reducing manual labeling effort and improving accuracy across the board.

This approach is interesting because it sidesteps the latency problem entirely. Online ad serving has hard millisecond budgets that LLMs can't meet, but offline tasks have much more relaxed constraints. A content moderation batch that takes hours can afford per-item inference times of seconds. By targeting offline tasks, AdNanny gets the benefits of LLM reasoning without the serving cost problem.

Practical takeaways: For ad platforms with complex offline pipelines (policy enforcement, ad quality scoring, relevance labeling for training data), a unified LLM backbone can reduce operational complexity. The key engineering challenges are the multi-task training recipe — getting the loss weighting right across diverse tasks — and the serving infrastructure for batch inference at scale. The DeepSeek-R1 base model choice suggests that reasoning capability (not just instruction following) matters for these offline tasks, likely because ad policy enforcement requires multi-step logical reasoning about edge cases.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.01563

item.title: RIA: Ranking-Infused Listwise CTR Prediction at Meituan
item.description:
Most ad ranking systems treat ranking and reranking as separate stages — a pointwise ranker scores individual items, then a listwise reranker adjusts for position bias and inter-item dependencies. Meituan's RIA (Ranking-Infused Approach) unifies these into a single end-to-end framework, and the online results show this matters.

The problem with decoupled ranking and reranking is information loss. The pointwise ranker produces scores without considering what other items are in the candidate set, and the reranker has to reconstruct context that was already available upstream. RIA shares representations between the two stages, allowing contextual knowledge to flow from listwise evaluation back into the pointwise scoring.

The architecture has four components. UCDT (User and Candidate DualTransformer) models user-item-context interactions — standard transformer attention over user features, candidate features, and contextual signals. CUHT (Context-aware User History and Target) captures position-sensitive preferences by modeling how user interest varies depending on where in the list an item appears. This is important because user attention drops off sharply with position, and the optimal item to show first depends on what else is in the candidate set.

LMH (Listwise Multi-HSTU) captures hierarchical item dependencies — essentially modeling how the value of showing item A depends on whether items B and C are also shown. This is the component that enables true listwise optimization within the ranking stage rather than as a post-hoc reranking step. EC (Embedding Cache) handles the efficiency problem: sharing representations across stages means computing them once and reusing, reducing the overhead of the unified approach.

Results: Deployed in Meituan's advertising system, RIA achieved +1.69% CTR improvement and +4.54% CPM increase in online A/B tests. The CPM lift is particularly notable — it suggests the listwise optimization is not just improving click prediction accuracy but also shifting the ranking toward higher-value impressions.

Why this matters for practitioners: The two-stage rank-then-rerank pattern is nearly universal in ad systems. RIA shows that unifying these stages can deliver meaningful online gains, but the engineering cost is real — you need to maintain shared representations, handle the latency of listwise computation, and manage the complexity of end-to-end training across what were previously independent systems. The 4.54% CPM lift suggests the ROI is there for platforms with sufficient engineering resources. For smaller teams, the CUHT position-sensitivity module alone might be worth extracting as a standalone improvement.

item.title: Bidding-Aware Retrieval: Bridging Auto-Bidding and Retrieval at Alibaba
item.description:
Auto-bidding has become the dominant way advertisers manage their campaigns — they set a target ROI or CPA, and the platform's bidding system adjusts bids in real time. But there's a fundamental mismatch: the retrieval stage, which selects which ads to consider for ranking, has no access to these dynamic bids. Alibaba's Bidding-Aware Retrieval (BAR) fixes this by incorporating bid value directly into the retrieval scoring function.

The problem is architectural. In most ad systems, retrieval is model-based — a two-tower or ANN-based system that retrieves candidates based on user-ad relevance. But relevance and value are different things. An ad with moderate relevance but a high auto-bid might be more valuable to show than a highly relevant ad with a low bid. Without bid information in retrieval, the system can miss high-value candidates that never make it to the ranking stage.

BAR introduces monotonicity-constrained learning to ensure the retrieval score is economically coherent — higher bids should not decrease the retrieval score, all else being equal. This is a non-trivial constraint because naively adding bid as a feature can cause the model to overfit to bid amounts rather than learning the interaction between relevance and value. The monotonicity constraint ensures the model respects the economic ordering while still learning nuanced relevance patterns.

The system also uses multi-task distillation to transfer knowledge from the ranking model back to the retrieval model. The ranking model has access to detailed features that retrieval can't use (too expensive at scale), so distilling ranking signals into retrieval helps close the information gap between the two stages.

Asynchronous near-line inference keeps the retrieval embeddings up to date as bids change. Auto-bids can shift minute-to-minute based on budget pacing and competition, so the retrieval model needs to reflect current market conditions. The near-line system updates embeddings asynchronously, avoiding the latency cost of real-time inference while staying responsive to market dynamics.

A Task-Attentive Refinement module selectively enhances feature interactions to disentangle user interest signals from commercial value signals. This is important because the model needs to reason about both "does this user want this ad?" and "is this ad worth showing?" as separate but related questions.

Results: Deployed across Alibaba's display advertising platform, BAR achieved 4.32% platform revenue increase and 22.2% impression lift for positively-operated advertisements. The impression lift for operated ads is particularly telling — it means advertisers who actively manage their campaigns are getting significantly more exposure, which improves the platform's advertiser satisfaction metrics.

For practitioners: If your ad system uses auto-bidding and has a separate retrieval stage, there's almost certainly a gap between what retrieval selects and what would be most valuable to rank. BAR's approach of making retrieval bidding-aware, with monotonicity constraints for economic sanity, is a template worth studying. The 4.32% revenue lift from retrieval-stage changes alone is unusually large — typically retrieval improvements are measured in basis points.

item.title: Click A Buy B: Rethinking Conversion Attribution in E-Commerce with Multi-Task CVR Prediction
item.description:
Researchers published a study on the Click A, Buy B (CABB) phenomenon in e-commerce, where users click product A but buy product B. The multi-task learning framework achieved -13.9% normalized entropy reduction offline and +0.25% primary business metric gains in online A/B testing.

Traditional conversion prediction models assume clicked and purchased items are the same (one-to-one mapping), causing biased learning and sub-optimal conversion rates. In reality, users often discover a better alternative after clicking — they click on a red shirt but buy a blue one from a different listing.

The paper reframes conversion prediction as a multi-task problem with two separate prediction heads: CABA (Click A, Buy A) for aligned conversions and CABB (Click A, Buy B) for cross-item conversions. A taxonomy-aware collaborative filtering weighting scheme maps each product to a leaf node in a product taxonomy and learns a category-to-category similarity matrix from large-scale co-engagement logs.

This weighting amplifies pairs that reflect genuine substitutable or complementary relations while down-weighting coincidental cross-category purchases. The system can distinguish between meaningful cross-item conversions (user clicked running shoes, bought similar running shoes) and noise (user clicked shoes, bought groceries).

The 13.9% NE reduction offline is substantial, and the 0.25% business metric improvement in online A/B testing demonstrates real-world value. For practitioners, this work highlights that conversion attribution is more complex than simple last-click models assume, and modeling cross-item conversion patterns can improve CVR prediction accuracy.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15113

item.title: ESCIM: Post-Click CVR Prediction via Counterfactual Inference with Structural Causal Models (ICDM 2025)
item.description:
Researchers published ESCIM (Entire Space Counterfactual Inference Multi-task Model) for CVR prediction, accepted at IEEE ICDM 2025. The approach uses counterfactual inference to generate conversion labels for non-clicked samples, addressing the fundamental sparsity problem in CVR prediction.

CVR models are traditionally trained solely on clicked samples, as conversions can only be determined following clicks. This creates a severe sparsity issue — only a small fraction of impressions lead to clicks, and only a small fraction of clicks lead to conversions. ESCIM asks: "Would the user have converted if he or she had clicked the recommended item?"

The approach uses a Structural Causal Model (SCM) trained on user sequential behaviors, applies a hypothetical intervention (do-calculus-style click intervention) on non-clicked items to infer counterfactual CVRs, and transforms predicted counterfactual CVRs into binary counterfactual conversion labels for sample augmentation.

This counterfactual approach dramatically expands the effective training set — instead of training only on the sparse clicked-and-converted samples, the model can learn from the entire impression space by inferring what would have happened if users had clicked.

The paper demonstrates superiority on public datasets and online A/B testing, with robust generalization capabilities on latent conversion data. For practitioners, ESCIM offers a principled approach to the data sparsity problem that plagues CVR prediction, using causal inference rather than simple negative sampling.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04816

item.title: Offline RL for Production Bidding Policies: Hybrid Agent Architecture for Ad Auctions
item.description:
Researchers published a method for optimizing production bidding policies using offline reinforcement learning. The approach achieved statistically significant performance gains in both simulated and at-scale production bidding environments, without requiring additional infrastructure, safety, or explainability costs.

The key innovation is a hybrid agent architecture combining base policies (differentiable heuristic policies that are explainable and already in production) with deep neural networks used during training only. Only the optimized base policy parameters are eventually deployed — the neural network part is discarded after training.

This design addresses a critical tension in ad tech: platforms own the bidding agents but use advertiser funds. The agents must be reliable and explainable, but also optimized for performance. By using neural networks only during training and deploying only the optimized heuristic parameters, the approach maintains the explainability and safety of production systems.

The method only requires data generated by the base policy itself — no environment interaction or online experimentation is needed. This is crucial for ad systems where online experimentation is expensive (every suboptimal bid costs real money) and potentially harmful to advertiser outcomes.

The approach optimizes any differentiable base policy by learning improved parameters from logged interactions, making it applicable to a wide range of existing bidding strategies.

For practitioners, this work demonstrates that offline RL can be safely applied to production bidding systems without the risks associated with online RL. The hybrid architecture — using neural networks for learning and heuristics for deployment — is a practical pattern for applying ML to safety-critical ad tech systems.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.09426

item.title: MIM: Multi-Modal Content Interest Modeling for CTR Prediction at Taobao
item.description:
Most CTR prediction models rely heavily on ID embeddings — learned vectors for each user and item that capture collaborative signals from interaction history. The problem is that ID embeddings are opaque: they encode patterns from past clicks but say nothing about why a user clicked. Taobao's MIM (Multi-modal Content Interest Modeling) paradigm replaces this with a three-stage pipeline that grounds user interest in actual content — images, titles, and other modalities.

The first stage is pre-training foundational models on domain-specific data to extract multi-modal embeddings. This is not just running CLIP on product images — the pre-training is adapted to Taobao's e-commerce domain, so the embeddings capture commercially relevant visual and textual features (brand logos, product categories, style attributes) rather than generic image semantics.

The second stage, Content-Interest-Aware Supervised Fine-Tuning (C-SFT), bridges the semantic gap between content features and user behavior signals. Raw multi-modal embeddings from a pretrained model encode content similarity, but user interest is more nuanced — two visually similar products might have very different click rates depending on price, brand, and context. C-SFT uses user behavior signals to fine-tune the multi-modal embeddings so they align with actual user preferences rather than just content similarity.

The third stage, Content-Interest-Aware User Behavior Modeling (CiUBM), integrates the fine-tuned multi-modal embeddings with traditional ID-based collaborative filtering signals in a unified framework. The key insight is that neither modality alone is sufficient — ID embeddings capture collaborative signals that content features miss (e.g., "users who bought X also bought Y" even when X and Y look nothing alike), while content features provide grounding that ID embeddings lack (especially for cold-start items with no interaction history).

Results: After online deployment on Taobao, MIM achieved +14.14% CTR increase and +4.12% RPM (Revenue Per Mille) increase. These are substantial numbers for a CTR model change on one of the world's largest e-commerce platforms. The RPM lift confirms that the CTR improvement is not just engagement noise — it translates to actual revenue.

The authors also released code and datasets, which is notable for an industrial paper.

Practical implications: The 14% CTR lift from incorporating multi-modal content signals is a strong signal that ID-only models are leaving significant performance on the table. For platforms with rich visual content (e-commerce, social, classified ads), the MIM pipeline — domain-adapted pre-training, behavior-aligned fine-tuning, unified integration — is a proven template. The engineering investment is substantial (three-stage training pipeline, multi-modal serving infrastructure), but the numbers suggest it's well worth it for large-scale platforms.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00321

item.title: RankMixer: Hardware-Aware Ranking Model Scaling at ByteDance
item.description:
Scaling up ranking models in ad systems is harder than it sounds. Transformers promise better feature interactions through self-attention, but in practice, industrial ranking models inherited from the CPU era have dismal Model Flops Utilization (MFU) — as low as 4.5% on modern GPUs. ByteDance's RankMixer tackles this by redesigning the ranking architecture for hardware efficiency, achieving 100x parameter scaling without increasing inference latency.

The core diagnosis is that existing ranking models waste most of their compute. Feature interaction modules designed for CPUs don't exploit GPU parallelism, and the embedding-heavy architecture creates memory bottlenecks that leave arithmetic units idle. RankMixer addresses this with a hardware-aware model design that retains transformer-style parallelism but replaces quadratic self-attention with a multi-head token mixing module for higher efficiency.

The token mixing module operates on feature tokens — each feature (user ID, item category, context, etc.) is a token, and the module learns to mix information across tokens without the O(n²) attention cost. Per-token FFNs maintain modeling for distinct feature subspaces while allowing cross-feature interactions. This design achieves much better hardware utilization because the computation is more regular and memory-access-friendly than attention.

The Sparse-MoE variant extends this to one billion parameters using a dynamic routing strategy. The key challenge with MoE in ranking is expert imbalance — some experts get overloaded while others are underutilized, especially since ad traffic has strong temporal patterns (morning vs. evening users have different feature distributions). The dynamic routing addresses this by adapting expert allocation based on input characteristics.

Results: The numbers tell the story clearly. MFU went from 4.5% to 45% — a 10x improvement in hardware utilization. The system scaled parameters by 100x while maintaining roughly the same inference latency. This was validated on a trillion-scale production dataset with online A/B tests across both Recommendation and Advertisement scenarios. The 1B dense-parameter RankMixer was launched for full traffic serving without increasing serving cost. Business impact: +0.3% user active days and +1.08% total in-app usage duration.

Why this matters: The 4.5% MFU figure should alarm anyone working on ad ranking systems. If your model is only using 4.5% of your GPU's compute capacity, you're paying for 22x more hardware than you need for the same model capacity. RankMixer's approach — redesigning the architecture for hardware efficiency rather than just throwing more GPUs at a poorly-utilized model — is the right long-term strategy. The 100x parameter scaling at constant latency means you can build much more expressive models within existing serving budgets. For teams planning their next-generation ranking architecture, RankMixer's token mixing approach is worth evaluating against standard transformer attention.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15551

item.title: NEZHA: Hyperspeed Decoding for Generative Recommendations on Taobao
item.description:
Generative recommendation models — those that generate candidate items autoregressively rather than scoring them from an embedding table — face a fundamental serving challenge: autoregressive decoding is sequential, and each generation step adds latency. Taobao's NEZHA solves this with a speculative decoding approach that achieves high throughput without sacrificing recommendation quality.

Standard speculative decoding uses a separate draft model (smaller, faster) to generate candidate token sequences, then verifies them in parallel with the main model. The problem is that maintaining two models doubles training cost and adds serving complexity — you need to keep both models loaded, manage their versioning, and handle cases where the draft model's predictions diverge from the main model.

NEZHA eliminates the separate draft model by integrating a nimble autoregressive draft head directly into the primary model. This self-drafting approach shares the main model's representations, so the draft head benefits from the full model's learned features without requiring its own separate processing. The draft head is lightweight — a small MLP or attention layer — so it adds minimal parameters and latency.

The system uses a specialized input prompt structure that preserves the integrity of sequence-to-sequence generation. In generative recommendation, the input is typically a sequence of user interactions, and the output is a sequence of recommended item tokens. The prompt structure ensures that the draft head generates tokens that are consistent with this seq2seq format, avoiding the coherence problems that can arise when a lightweight head tries to predict tokens in a complex generation task.

For hallucination prevention — a real concern when generating item IDs, since invalid IDs would cause serving failures — NEZHA uses an efficient, model-free verifier based on a hash set. Rather than running a neural network to verify generated tokens, it simply checks whether each generated token corresponds to a valid item in the catalog. This is O(1) per token and adds negligible latency.

Deployment: NEZHA has been serving on Taobao since October 2025, driving billion-level advertising revenue and serving hundreds of millions of daily active users.

Why this is notable: The self-drafting approach is elegant — by folding the draft head into the main model, you get speculative decoding's throughput benefits without the operational complexity of maintaining two models. The hash-set verifier is a pragmatic engineering choice: for item token generation, you don't need a neural verifier when a simple lookup suffices. For teams deploying generative retrieval, NEZHA demonstrates that the latency problem is solvable without doubling your model infrastructure. The billion-level revenue figure confirms this is not just a research prototype but a system handling real production traffic at scale.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.18793

item.title: MLCC: Multi-Level Compression Cross Networks for Efficient CTR/CVR at Bilibili
item.description:
Feature interaction modeling is the backbone of CTR and CVR prediction, but high-order feature crosses are expensive. Cross Networks (DCN and variants) can model arbitrary-order interactions, but the parameter count and compute grow rapidly with interaction order. Bilibili's MLCC (Multi-Level Compression Cross) tackles this with hierarchical compression that captures high-order dependencies at a fraction of the cost.

The core idea is organizing feature crosses through hierarchical compression and dynamic composition. Instead of computing all possible high-order feature interactions explicitly, MLCC compresses them into a structured hierarchy where lower-order interactions are composed to form higher-order ones. This is more parameter-efficient than direct computation because shared lower-order components are reused across many higher-order interactions.

The multi-channel variant MC-MLCC decomposes feature interactions into parallel subspaces, each responsible for different aspects of feature interaction. This allows horizontal scaling — adding more channels increases modeling capacity without the quadratic parameter growth of naive approaches. The channels learn to specialize, with some focusing on user-item interactions and others on contextual feature crosses.

Results: MLCC outperforms strong DLRM baselines by up to 0.52 AUC while reducing model parameters and FLOPs by up to 26x under comparable performance. The scaling behavior is stable and predictable across embedding dimension, head number, and channel count — important for capacity planning. Channel-based scaling achieves substantially better efficiency than conventional embedding inflation (just making embeddings bigger).

Online A/B testing on Bilibili's ad platform confirmed practical effectiveness, and the approach has been widely adopted in Bilibili's advertising system.

Practical takeaways: The 26x parameter reduction at comparable AUC is a significant efficiency win. For ad platforms where serving costs are dominated by feature interaction computation, MLCC's hierarchical compression offers a way to maintain model quality while dramatically reducing infrastructure costs. The stable scaling behavior is equally important — being able to predict how performance changes with model size makes capacity planning much easier than architectures with unpredictable scaling. The multi-channel design is particularly relevant for platforms with diverse feature types (user, item, context, cross-features), as different channels can naturally specialize for different feature groups.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12041

item.title: D-MoE: De-Correlated Expert Networks for CTR Prediction at Tencent
item.description:
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) has become a standard scaling technique in ad ranking models — add more experts, route different inputs to different experts, increase capacity without proportional compute increase. But there's a well-known failure mode: expert collapse, where multiple experts learn nearly identical functions, wasting capacity. Tencent's D-MoE (De-Correlated MoE) addresses this with a principled approach to ensuring expert diversity.

The core contribution is a Cross-Expert De-Correlation loss that explicitly penalizes similarity between expert outputs during training. Rather than relying on the router to naturally discover diverse experts — which often fails because the router's gradients push experts toward similar high-performing functions — D-MoE directly optimizes for expert diversity. The loss measures pairwise correlation between expert outputs and adds a penalty term that increases as experts become more similar.

The authors also define a new Cross-Expert Correlation metric for quantitatively assessing how decorrelated the experts are. This is useful for monitoring during training — if correlation starts climbing, you know expert collapse is happening before it degrades model performance. The metric is simple to compute and can be tracked alongside standard training metrics.

An interesting finding is that different de-correlation strategies are mutually compatible. You can apply de-correlation at different levels — output-level, representation-level, routing-level — and combining them progressively leads to better performance than any single strategy. This compositional property means you can start with one de-correlation method and add others incrementally without destabilizing training.

Results: Online A/B test at Tencent advertising showed D-MoE achieves a 1.19% GMV (Gross Merchandise Volume) lift compared to the Multi-Embedding MoE baseline. GMV is the metric that matters most for e-commerce ad platforms — it measures actual transaction value, not just clicks or impressions.

Why this matters: Expert collapse is a silent killer in MoE models. You think you have a model with 8 experts providing 8x capacity, but in practice 3-4 of them are doing nearly the same thing. D-MoE's de-correlation loss is a simple, low-cost intervention that ensures you actually get the capacity you're paying for. The 1.19% GMV lift from what is essentially a regularization technique is a strong return on investment. For any team running MoE-based ranking models, adding a de-correlation loss should be considered a best practice — it's cheap to implement and the downside risk is minimal.

Sources:

item.title: GME: Graph Meta Embeddings for Cold-Start Ads in CTR Prediction (SIGIR 2021)
item.description:
Researchers published GME (Graph Meta Embeddings) for cold-start ads in CTR prediction. The approach significantly improves prediction performance over five major deep learning-based CTR prediction models in both cold-start and warm-up scenarios. The paper was accepted at SIGIR 2021.

Cold-start ads lack sufficient training data for their embeddings to be well-learned, causing deep learning CTR models to perform poorly. GME combines graph neural networks and meta learning to rapidly generate initial embeddings for new ad IDs.

The system leverages two information sources: the new ad's associated attributes and existing old ads. A graph connecting old ads with new ads is built, and the model adaptively distills useful information from neighbors. Three model variants are proposed:

  • GME-P: Uses pre-trained neighbor ID embeddings
  • GME-G: Generates embeddings for neighbor IDs
  • GME-A: Leverages attribute information from neighboring ads

Both cold-start (no training data available) and warm-up (a small number of training samples) scenarios are addressed. The approach also applies to conversion rate (CVR) prediction.

For practitioners, GME offers a practical solution to the cold-start problem that every ad system faces. When new ads are created, they need reasonable initial embeddings to participate in the ranking system. GME's graph-based meta-learning approach generates these embeddings from the ad's attributes and the structure of the existing ad graph.

Sources:

item.title: Confidence Ranking for CTR Prediction: Deployed at JD.com for Fine-Rank Stage (WWW 2023)
item.description:
JD.com deployed Confidence Ranking, a framework for CTR prediction that formulates the optimization objective as a ranking function combining two different models. The framework was deployed in JD.com's advertisement system to serve main traffic in the fine-rank stage. The paper was accepted at WWW 2023.

The key innovation is the confidence ranking loss, which allows direct optimization of the logits output for different convex surrogate functions. This enables selecting the optimization target (AUC or Accuracy) depending on the task and dataset, rather than being locked into a fixed loss function.

The framework addresses the practical challenge of model evolution in production systems. JD.com uses periodic retraining with all data combined with online learning on recent data to handle the constant availability of new data. The confidence ranking approach integrates well with this continuous training setup.

For practitioners, Confidence Ranking demonstrates that the loss function choice in CTR prediction should be task-dependent. Different ad products and surfaces may benefit from different optimization objectives, and a flexible framework that can switch between objectives is valuable.

item.title: DoorDash Ads: Transitioning from Tree-Based Models to Multi-Task DNNs for Conversion Prediction
item.description:
DoorDash published their experience applying deep learning to ads conversion prediction in their last-mile delivery marketplace, transitioning from traditional tree-based models to cutting-edge multi-task DNNs. The paper describes improvements across data foundations, model design, training efficiency, evaluation rigor, and online serving.

The unique challenge of a delivery marketplace is that conversions (orders) have a complex relationship with ad exposure. Unlike e-commerce where the clicked product is often the purchased product, delivery marketplace conversions involve a restaurant being ordered from — which may happen through organic discovery or ad-driven discovery.

DoorDash's multi-task DNN approach predicts multiple objectives simultaneously, capturing the relationships between different user actions (viewing a restaurant, adding items, completing an order). This multi-objective approach is particularly valuable in delivery marketplaces where the conversion funnel has multiple stages.

The transition from tree-based models (LightGBM, XGBoost) to DNNs is a common trajectory in ad tech, but DoorDash's experience provides practical insights into the challenges and benefits of this transition in a delivery marketplace context.

For practitioners, this paper offers a case study of applying modern DNN-based ad ranking to a delivery marketplace — a domain with unique characteristics compared to traditional display advertising or e-commerce.

Sources:

item.title: IDProxy: Cold-Start CTR Prediction at Xiaohongshu with Multimodal LLMs for Hundreds of Millions of Users
item.description:
Xiaohongshu (Little Red Book) deployed IDProxy, a system that uses multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to generate proxy embeddings for cold-start items in CTR prediction. The system serves hundreds of millions of users daily across both Content Feed and Display Ads.

The cold-start problem is acute in advertising: new ads lack user interaction history, making it difficult to generate accurate CTR predictions. IDProxy addresses this by using MLLMs to generate proxy embeddings from content signals (images, text, metadata) for new items that lack usage history.

The key design principle is that proxy embeddings are explicitly aligned with the existing ID embedding space and optimized end-to-end under CTR objectives together with the ranking model. This ensures that the proxy embeddings are compatible with the rest of the ranking system and improve CTR prediction accuracy.

The system is designed for seamless integration into existing large-scale ranking pipelines, avoiding the need for major architectural changes. This is critical for production deployment — any cold-start solution that requires significant pipeline changes is unlikely to be adopted.

For practitioners, IDProxy demonstrates that multimodal LLMs can be practically applied to the cold-start problem in ad ranking. The key insight is using LLMs to generate embeddings that are aligned with the existing embedding space, rather than trying to replace the entire ranking model with an LLM.

Sources:

item.title: KuaiFormer: Transformer-Based Retrieval at Kuaishou for 400M Daily Active Users
item.description:
Kuaishou deployed KuaiFormer, a transformer-based retrieval framework replacing traditional dual-tower approaches for their short-video recommendation system. Integrated since May 2024, the system serves over 400 million daily active users and has driven a marked increase in average daily usage time.

KuaiFormer represents a paradigm shift from conventional score estimation tasks (such as CTR estimation) to a transformer-driven Next Action Prediction paradigm. This enables more effective real-time interest acquisition and multi-interest extraction from user behavior sequences.

The retrieval stage is the initial stage in the recommendation pipeline, responsible for selecting thousands of candidate items from billions of options. Traditional dual-tower models compute user and item embeddings independently and match them via dot product, limiting the interaction between user and item features.

KuaiFormer's transformer-based approach enables richer user-item interaction during retrieval, capturing more nuanced user interests. The deployment at Kuaishou — one of the largest short-video platforms globally — validates that transformer architectures can work at massive scale for retrieval tasks.

For practitioners, KuaiFormer demonstrates that the transformer revolution is extending beyond ranking to retrieval. The ability to perform richer user-item matching during retrieval can improve the quality of candidates passed to the ranking stage, potentially improving overall recommendation quality.

Sources:

item.title: Efficient Embedding-Based Ad Retrieval with GPU-Powered Feature Interaction at Tencent
item.description:
Tencent deployed an GPU-accelerated feature interaction mechanism for dual-tower networks in their advertising recommendation system, delivering significant online performance gains. This is the first successful implementation of Wide and Deep architecture within a retrieval system.

Traditional dual-tower models compute user and ad embeddings independently, with interactions only at the final inner product computation. This yields insufficient feature interaction capabilities — the model cannot capture complex user-ad relationships that require early interaction between features.

The proposed solution uses a novel compressed inverted list designed for GPU acceleration, enabling efficient feature interaction computation at scale. By bringing early-stage user-ad interaction — normally only feasible in ranking with DNN models — into the retrieval stage, the system captures richer patterns without sacrificing retrieval speed.

The deployment at Tencent's advertising recommendation system validates that GPU-powered feature interaction can work at industrial scale. The significant online performance gains demonstrate that investing in retrieval quality — not just ranking quality — pays off in production ad systems.

For practitioners, this work demonstrates that the retrieval stage can be enhanced with more sophisticated feature interactions using GPU acceleration. The compressed inverted list technique enables efficient nearest-neighbor search with feature interaction, opening new possibilities for retrieval model design.

Sources:

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.22460
